extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, advanced fiction students, and fiction writers interested in narrative technique and rhetorical principles of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Wayne C. Booth's criteria for evaluating and producing fictional narrative, especially voice, point of view, and rhetorical effects on readers. Useful for critics, teachers, and writers who assess narrative reliability, distance, and authorial presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling and Showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between 'telling' (authoritative narration) and 'showing' (dramatic presentation) as fundamental modes of fictional presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate when an author 'tells' facts or judgments directly versus when events are dramatized for readers to infer meaning. Consider effects on reader belief, distance, and control of interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative 'Telling' in Early Narration
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of an authoritative telling voice in earlier narrative practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how an authoritative narrator supplies facts or interpretation and how that authority shapes reader expectations and perceived reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Author’s Many Voices
rubrics_metrics.description: A work may contain multiple authorial voices rather than a single uniform voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between the implied author, narrative speaker(s), and other voices; evaluate coherence, contrast, and purpose of multiple voices within a text.

rubrics_metrics.name: "True Novels Must Be Realistic" (General Rules I)
rubrics_metrics.description: The historical/aesthetic rule that 'true' novels should be realistic, including concerns such as the novel as unmediated reality and ordering of intensities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a work against realism expectations: intensity of realistic fiction, whether the novel presents itself as unmediated reality, and how to discriminate among different kinds/levels of realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of General Criteria: Work, Author, Reader
rubrics_metrics.description: General criteria for fiction derive from three sources: the work itself, the author, and the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a text, consider norms arising from the internal work, authorial intentions/stance (implied author), and readerly conventions or expectations (postulated reader).

rubrics_metrics.name: "All Authors Should be Objective" (General Rules II)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule that authors should be objective — including neutrality, the author's 'second self', impartiality, and impassibilité.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine claims to authorial neutrality and the techniques that produce perceived impartiality; note when impersonal techniques actually encourage subjectivism or obscure responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: "True Art Ignores the Audience" (General Rules III)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that 'true artists write only for themselves' and the debate over whether pure fiction ignoring audience expectations is theoretically desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tensions between 'pure' art and 'impurity' (writing for audience), and whether writing that disregards audience leads to greater aesthetic value or alienation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotions, Beliefs, and the Reader’s Objectivity (General Rules IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relationship among emotional response, belief, and the reader's supposed objectivity — including types of literary interest and distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how a text solicits tears, laughter, belief, or distance; consider Booth's warning that 'tears and laughter are, aesthetically, frauds' and analyze combinations/conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Narration (person, dramatized/undramatized, observers, agents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxonomy of narration: person (first/third), dramatized vs undramatized narrators, observers vs narrator-agents, scene vs summary, commentary, self-conscious narrators, variations of distance, privilege, and inside views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify narration type(s) used and evaluate effects on access to character consciousness, credibility, distance, and reader alignment; analyze scene vs summary choices and presence of self-conscious commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene versus Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal distinction between dramatized 'scene' and authorial 'summary' as modes for presenting events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge when an author chooses to dramatize events or compress them into summary and how that choice alters pacing, immersion, and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of Reliable Commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions of reliable authorial commentary: providing facts/picture/summary, molding beliefs, relating particulars to established norms, heightening significance, generalizing events or the whole work, manipulating mood, and commenting directly on the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commentary is present, evaluate which of these functions it serves and whether it strengthens or weakens reader response and interpretive clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatized Narrators: Reliable and Unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatized narrators can be reliable or unreliable; reliable narrators can serve as dramatized spokesmen for the implied author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess narrator reliability and how dramatized narration aligns with or diverges from the implied author's norms. Use historical examples (e.g., Fielding in Tom Jones, Tristram Shandy) to evaluate formal coherence and good/bad commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of Distance (sympathy and judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's control of narrative distance to produce sympathy, judgment, and inside views (exemplified in Jane Austen's Emma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how distance is manipulated to shape readers' sympathy or moral judgment, how inside views create intimacy, and how control of judgment is established by narrative technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Implied Author as Friend and Guide
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept that an implied author can function as a guiding presence who mediates judgment and relationship between text and reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how the implied author’s stance subtly instructs readers in how to interpret characters and events, and whether that guidance is overt or covert.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Uses of Authorial Silence
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques in which the author 'exits' or remains silent: using silence to control sympathy, clarity/confusion, and to create a 'secret communion' between author and reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze moments where authorial comment is withheld and the rhetorical effects—increasing ambiguity, inviting inference, inducing complicity between author and reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion of Distance and Irony (Price of Impersonal Narration I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that arise from impersonal narration, including confusion of distance and troubles with irony (examples: The Turn of the Screw; A Portrait of the Artist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When narration is impersonal, assess risks of puzzlement, misreadings of irony, or uncertain normative stance; ask whether confusion is accidental or purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable Narrator Development (Price of Impersonal Narration II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Development of unreliable narrators (e.g., Henry James) from flawed reflectors into subjects of narrative; issues of formal coherence and reader response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how unreliability is constructed, whether it signals authorial judgment, and its formal consequences for unity and interpretative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality of Impersonal Narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Relationship between narrative technique and moral judgment: how impersonal narration can obscure the author’s moral stance and the 'morality of elitism' or seductive points of view (example: Céline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ethical implications of point of view choices: does technique mask endorsement of morally dubious perspectives? Does the narrative encourage elitism or seduction of problematic attitudes?

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts: 'Implied Author', 'Postulated Reader', 'Unreliable Narrator'
rubrics_metrics.description: Key conceptual tools: the implied author (a constructed authorial presence), the postulated reader (the reader the text anticipates), and the unreliable narrator as standard critical vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these concepts to analyze authorial intention as inferred from the text, the expectations set for readers, and the consequences of narrative unreliability for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulating Mood and Molding Beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques by which narration and commentary shape the reader's mood and beliefs about events and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate specific devices (tone, selective detail, commentary) that steer belief and mood, and judge whether such manipulation is rhetorically effective or ethically problematic.
